examples: I have to wear a uniform at work. It's the company rule.
I must buy a new shirt — this one is too old now.
When I was at school we had to wear a horrible uniform.
You don't have to pay — this museum is free.
You mustn't park here. It's a bus stop.
You should take warm clothes with you to Dublin. It might be cold at night.
A pilot has to wear a uniform when he's at work.
We don't have to hurry. We have plenty of time.
grammar.explanation: We use have to and must + infinitive to talk about obligation — when something is necessary to do. They usually mean the same thing, but have to is more common for general or external rules (I have to wear a shirt and tie at work), while must is more common for personal or specific decisions (I must buy a new shirt — this one is too old now). have to is a normal verb, so it exists in all tenses and forms: I had to get up early yesterday; She has to work nights sometimes. must is a modal verb — it only exists in the present, but it can have a future meaning (You must be on time tomorrow). Do not confuse don't have to with mustn't. don't have to means there is no obligation — you can do it if you want (You don't have to pay — this museum is free). mustn't means prohibition — you are not allowed to do it (You mustn't park here; You mustn't send text messages when you are driving). We use should / shouldn't + infinitive to give advice or an opinion. It is weaker than must or have to (You should take warm clothes with you to Dublin; You shouldn't drink so much coffee). ought to is a more formal alternative to should (You ought to take warm clothes with you).
